June 15, 2026 
Dr. Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: CMS-0062-P  
Submitted electronically to: http://www.regulations.gov 
 
 
Dear Administrator Oz: 
We applaud CMS for taking a leadership role in ensuring that patients, along with many other 
entities in the health system, can leverage digital technologies to access the information they 
need to make good healthcare choices. 
 
Organizational Background 
Checkbookâ€™s organizational mission is to help consumers make educated and high-value choices 
of service providers. In the course of this work, we have observed many problems associated 
with access to information about insurance plans and in-network providers. We have long 
advocated for transparency and accessibility of information consumers need to make educated 
choices of healthcare services and service providers. 
 
Below we provide more detailed comments regarding the proposed rules. 
 
We welcome the opportunity to engage further with CMS on this subject â€“ please do not 
hesitate to contact Eric Ellsworth at eellsworth@checkbook.org or 202-454-3010 if you have 
any questions or we can provide further information or assistance. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Need for Centralized Collection and Publication of API Endpoints in the National 
Provider Directory 
We strongly support the collection and publication of impacted payersâ€™ API endpoints in the 
National Provider Directory. We do not support the alternative approach of self-publication 
through NDH IG Endpoint Profile, for several reasons. First, this would leave the task of 
discovering the correct NDH Endpoint resources to stakeholders such as app developers, 
patients, researchers and others. Second, the lack of a regular, time-driven collection process 
would reduce the accountability for making updates to publicly posted information on a regular 
basis. Third, collecting URLs will allow CMS to engage in ongoing monitoring and testing of 
endpoint availability and standards conformance, similar to the way ONCâ€™s Lantern system 
monitors EHR endpoint availability and conformance. 
A similar CMS collection and discovery resource, the CCIIO Machine Readable URL PUF, serves 
as an indispensable resource for our work collecting, cleansing, and publishing provider 
directory data from payersâ€™ QHP JSON files for our plan shopping tools. CCIIOâ€™s published list of 
URLs serves as an authoritative definition of the location of URLs for the QHP JSON files, with 
QHP issuers accountable to both CMS and the public for stale or incorrect results. By contrast, 
in State-Based Marketplaces, where the files are not required to be submitted, we must directly 
contact payers when such URLs are not discoverable, become stale or non-functional, or have 
changed. We believe that having multiple entities attempt this sort of coordination with payers 
is inefficient for all parties involved. Additionally, we have encountered cases where payers are 
not responsive until we involve an entity to whom they are accountable. A regular, centralized 
collection and publication process would ensure that the endpoints are maintained in an 
accurate and up-to-date state. 
We further suggest that CMS request voluntary submission of payersâ€™ API endpoints for non-
impacted market segments/Lines of Business (LOBs). In most cases, a given payer will maintain 
the same endpoint across many plans within an LOB, and many payers maintain the same 
endpoint across multiple or all LOBs. However, unless the endpoint that it can be used for a 
non-impacted LOB (e.g. ERISA-regulated plans) is asserted in a centralized location like that 
National Provider Directory, any app developer will have to have a process to confirm that it is 
the correct endpoint for non-impacted LOBs. 
A comprehensive directory would: 
- 
Streamline consumer access to insurance information across the entire market 
- 
Dramatically improve the reach and coverage of the information and coverage of apps 
built against the FHIR APIs and drive market discipline for insurers to expose accurate, 
timely information through all APIS 
- 
Reduce the burden on consumers, providers, and others in understanding different 
procedures, apps, for different market segments 
 
 
 
 
Urgent Need for Well-Structured Network, Plan, and Payer Identifiers 
To fully empower consumers to make informed, value-oriented decisions in healthcare there 
remains an urgent need for a clear network-based product identifier that permits a consumer 
to access key details of their health plan and compatibility of the plan with providers, 
treatment, or services. Since shopping involves marshalling information in advance of making a 
purchase decision, such a product identifier must be open and not require going through a 
provider in order learn details of coverage and cost. 
Since much of the information consumers need to know about health plans will flow through 
the APIs mandated under CMS-0057 and these proposed rules, it is critical that consumers or 
apps acting on their behalf be able to seamlessly resolve which endpoints go with their specific 
health plan product.  
Additionally, such an identifier will dramatically improve the quality of the Transparency in 
Coverage (TIC) files. We, along price transparency data vendors and other stakeholders, noted in 
our comments about CMS-9882P that a well-structured network identifier is essential to make 
TIC files sufficiently accurate and linkable to other information to simplify consumer decisions. 
We also suggested a collaborative process for defining a workable standard for the identifier; we 
believe that this kind of stakeholder-driven effort aligns well with the aims of CMSâ€™ Health Tech 
Ecosystem. In conversations with ecosystem partners, some have proposed a strawman structure 
for such a network-based product identifier. We do not necessarily endorse this structure, but 
felt that it raises some significant issues worth consideration. 
Another key source of information which is needed to support consumers in making empowered, 
cost-conscious decisions about their care is the formulary status of medications they may be 
considering. Prior authorization requests for pharmacy dispensed medications make implicit use 
of a health planâ€™s formulary list of drug coverage. Seamless and transparent access to formularies 
helps consumers understand coverage in advance of making a prior authorization request, and 
to differentiate between a covered drug where prior authorization has been denied versus a non-
covered drug. 
Consumer access to formularies presently happens primarily through either PDF formularies or 
formulary lookup tools that payers make available online. Both the PDF formularies and lookup 
tools are also very poorly identified. Most publicly exposed information about formularies has no 
clear identifier; typically the only way that a consumer can know if this formulary goes with their 
plan is via link that they followed to that formulary from some plan-related document. Similar to 
the network-plan relationship, many plans often use the same formulary or a lightly-customized 
version of a base formulary. Plan and payer identifiers should enable consumers and apps to 
access the correct formulary ideally via the FHIR Formulary resource that pertains to the plan. 
 
 
 
We urge CMS to continue development of open and well-structured Payer, Network, and 
Plan identifiers across all markets. CMS should request that impacted payers voluntarily 
collaborate in extending such an identifier across all market segments, including non-impacted 
LOBs/market segments (mostly notable self-insured plans falling under ERISA regulation), and 
coordinate with relevant offices within the Department of Labor to maximize the reach of such 
an identifier. 
 
Collection of URLs for Transparency in Coverage (TIC) Files 
We suggest that the NPD should also collect URLs for Transparency in Coverage machine-
readable files price (â€œTIC filesâ€) for all impacted payers, and request voluntary submission of 
these URLS for non-impacted LOBs. The same challenges as occur in API endpoint discovery also 
apply to discovering TIC files, and are amplified because payers typically do not consolidate TIC 
files across plans or LOBs to the same degree as API endpoints. As such, discovering the URL for 
the relevant TIC file is burdensome and limit real-world access to these files those price 
transparency vendors and others with the resources and expertise to maintain URL discovery 
codebases. 
The TIC files contain information derived from the same provider-payer contracts that are used 
to populate payersâ€™ provider directories. When properly linked, the data in the TIC files can serve 
to validate provider directory data published through the NPD, as well as helping clarify the 
identity of networks for development and oversight of network, payer, and plan identifiers. 
Simplified discovery of and access to these files and the ability to link data in these files to the 
data in a provider directory can serve both for validation of provider directory data, and to enable 
consumers and app developers to combine prices from TIC files with verified provider-network 
participation location data as asserted in a provider directory API or the National Provider 
Directory.  
 
Collection of Reasons for Prior Authorization Denials Using Structure Codes 
We applaud the requirement for payers to provide clear explanations of the reason for denials 
of prior authorization. We suggest that CMS require payers to use well-structured reason codes 
alongside free text explanations of prior authorization denials. The X12 reason codes used in 
claims processing, including claim adjustment reason codes and group codes, claims status codes 
and category codes, remittance advice remark codes, and possibly provider adjustment reason 
codes provide an excellent framework for this type of structured data. X12 codes are already 
used within FHIR, and these codes could be augmented for any situations occurring only in prior 
authorization using existing processes for modifying X12 codesets. 
 
 
 
Experience in using claims denial data currently reported under the ACAâ€™s â€œTransparency 
in Coverageâ€ reporting requirements (these are not TIC files) suggests that without a code-based 
system, there will be much variability in how payers interpret reporting instructions. Lack of 
specificity in how to categorize the reasons for claims denials leaves confusion about initial 
denials vs final denials, and denial reasons, and who should be accountable, leading to vague and 
non-actionable public debate about the appropriate regulatory response for denials. 
A code-based system for reporting prior authorization denials can enable apples-to-apples 
comparisons of denials by well-defined categories of reasons. CMS should require reporting 
aggregated denial rates broken out by such reason codes. 
 
Alignment of Prior Authorization Timelines for QHPs with other impact payers 
We support aligning prior authorization timelines for QHPs with other impacted payers. A single 
standard across market segments will enable consumers to better understand their rights and 
take action, without having to navigate plan or market specific rules about when they should 
expect a response to prior authorization requests.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Consumers' Checkbook / Checkbook; contact Eric Ellsworth.
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group / Other (consumer information and plan/provider choice organization)
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Checkbook states its mission is helping consumers make educated, high-value choices of service providers and describes extensive experience collecting, cleansing, and publishing provider directory data from QHP JSON files for plan shopping tools.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Checkbook supports CMS's interoperability goals and specifically supports centralized CMS collection and publication of impacted payers' API endpoints in the National Provider Directory rather than decentralized self-publication. The comment also urges CMS to develop structured payer, network, plan, and formulary identifiers, collect Transparency in Coverage file URLs, require structured prior authorization denial reason codes, report denial rates by reason code, and align QHP prior authorization timelines with other impacted payers.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-USAGE-METRICS; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No CFR citations. The comment references CMS-0062-P, CMS-0057, CMS-9882P, ACA Transparency in Coverage reporting, Transparency in Coverage machine-readable files, and ERISA-regulated/self-insured plans.
- **Standards referenced:** National Provider Directory; NDH IG Endpoint Profile; FHIR APIs; FHIR Formulary resource; X12 claim adjustment reason codes, group codes, claims status codes/category codes, remittance advice remark codes, provider adjustment reason codes; CCIIO Machine Readable URL PUF; ONC Lantern.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Centralized API Endpoint Collection and Publication**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Checkbook argues that a centralized, time-driven CMS collection process would make endpoints easier for app developers, patients, and researchers to discover; create payer accountability; and enable CMS monitoring similar to ONC Lantern.
- **Specific request:** CMS should collect and publish impacted payer API endpoints in the National Provider Directory and should not rely on self-publication through the NDH IG Endpoint Profile as the primary approach.

**Topic 2: Voluntary Endpoint Submission for Non-Impacted Lines of Business**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Many payers use the same endpoints across plans and lines of business, but app developers cannot confidently use them for non-impacted lines without a centralized assertion.
- **Specific request:** CMS should request voluntary submission of API endpoints for non-impacted market segments, including ERISA-regulated plans, to broaden consumer access and app coverage.

**Topic 3: Payer, Network, Plan, and Formulary Identifiers**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** The commenter states that consumers and apps need open, structured identifiers to connect a health plan product to endpoints, provider networks, treatments, services, formularies, and price transparency data.
- **Specific request:** CMS should continue developing open, well-structured payer, network, and plan identifiers across all markets and coordinate with the Department of Labor to extend reach into self-insured ERISA plans.

**Topic 4: Transparency in Coverage URL Collection**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** TIC file discovery is burdensome, especially because payers often do not consolidate TIC files across plans and lines of business. Centralized URL collection would allow directories, TIC files, provider network participation, and prices to be linked and validated.
- **Specific request:** The National Provider Directory should collect TIC machine-readable file URLs for impacted payers and seek voluntary submissions for non-impacted lines of business.

**Topic 5: Structured Prior Authorization Denial Reason Codes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Free-text explanations alone would lead to inconsistent categorization and vague public debate, as seen in ACA denial reporting. Structured codes would support apples-to-apples analysis and accountability.
- **Specific request:** CMS should require well-structured denial reason codes alongside free text, using X12 code sets where possible and augmenting them as needed for prior authorization.

**Topic 6: Prior Authorization Timeline Alignment for QHPs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** A single standard across market segments would make consumer rights easier to understand and act upon.
- **Specific request:** CMS should align prior authorization timelines for QHPs with other impacted payers.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S16:** The comment responds directly by supporting clear explanations for prior authorization denials and recommending that explanations include structured denial reason codes.
- **S17:** The comment directly supports structured codes and recommends using existing X12 denial/remittance/status code frameworks, augmented where necessary for prior authorization.
- **S23:** The comment supports centralized endpoint publication and argues it improves discoverability and accountability; it does not identify security objections to publication.
- **S24:** The comment recommends that CMS collect payer API endpoint URLs and also voluntarily collect endpoint information for non-impacted lines of business.
- **S26:** The comment opposes relying primarily on self-publication through the NDH IG Endpoint Profile and favors centralized CMS/NPD collection and publication.
- **S27:** The comment supports a regular, time-driven collection process so endpoint information is updated and stale URLs can be corrected.
- **S29:** The comment proposes reporting aggregated prior authorization denial rates broken out by structured reason codes, which is a usage/accountability metric for PA processes.
- **S33:** The comment supports publishing API endpoint information through the National Provider Directory, analogous to the CCIIO Machine Readable URL PUF.
- **S40:** The comment indirectly supports broader market reach by recommending voluntary endpoint and identifier participation for non-impacted market segments and lines of business.
- **S43:** The comment supports aligning QHP prior authorization timelines with other impacted payers to simplify consumer understanding of rights.
- **S66-S82:** The comment raises broader interoperability issues around network, plan, payer, formulary, and TIC identifiers that support consumer choice beyond the narrow drug PA provisions.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Collect and publish impacted payers' API endpoints centrally in the National Provider Directory.
2. Do not rely on decentralized self-publication through the NDH IG Endpoint Profile as the primary endpoint discovery mechanism.
3. Use centralized endpoint collection to enable ongoing CMS monitoring and conformance testing similar to ONC Lantern.
4. Request voluntary endpoint submissions for non-impacted market segments and lines of business, including ERISA-regulated plans.
5. Develop open, structured payer, network, and plan identifiers across all markets.
6. Coordinate with the Department of Labor to maximize use of identifiers in self-insured ERISA markets.
7. Improve formulary identification and support access to the correct plan-specific formulary, ideally through FHIR Formulary resources.
8. Collect TIC machine-readable file URLs through the National Provider Directory.
9. Link TIC files, provider directory data, and identifiers to validate directory data and enable price/network tools.
10. Require structured prior authorization denial reason codes alongside free-text explanations.
11. Require reporting of aggregated denial rates by reason code.
12. Align QHP prior authorization timelines with other impacted payers.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Endpoint self-publication would reduce discoverability and accountability; network/plan/payer/formulary identifiers are inadequate; TIC URLs are hard to discover; free-text denial explanations would be inconsistent; QHP-specific timelines confuse consumers.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** App developers and consumers may be unable to find correct endpoints or TIC files; consumers may not be able to determine provider compatibility, treatment coverage, formulary status, or cost; denial data may be vague and non-comparable.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Stale or undiscoverable URLs, payer non-responsiveness without CMS accountability, lack of identifiers across non-impacted markets, poor formulary identification, inconsistent denial categorization, and lack of a regular endpoint update process.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** No quantitative statistics cited.
- **Studies or research referenced:** No formal studies cited.
- **Examples provided:** Checkbook cites its use of the CCIIO Machine Readable URL PUF for QHP JSON files and contrasts it with State-Based Marketplaces where URLs are not centrally submitted and require direct payer outreach. It also references experience with ACA Transparency in Coverage denial reporting to show variability when code-based categories are absent.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Consumers, patients, app developers, researchers, payers, QHP issuers, ERISA/self-insured plan sponsors, CMS, Department of Labor, price transparency vendors, providers, and entities using the National Provider Directory.
- **Economic implications:** Centralized endpoint and TIC URL discovery would reduce duplicative URL discovery work and improve market efficiency for consumer tools. Structured identifiers and denial codes could reduce administrative ambiguity and improve accountability.
- **Technical feasibility:** The commenter frames the approach as feasible by analogy to the existing CCIIO URL PUF and ONC Lantern, and recommends using existing X12 code sets and FHIR resources where possible.
- **Patient care impact:** Better endpoint discovery, identifiers, formularies, and PA denial transparency would help consumers understand coverage, access correct information, compare plans/providers, and exercise rights under prior authorization timelines.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with modifications.
- **Tone:** Professional, constructive, and policy-focused.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "We strongly support the collection and publication of impacted payers' API endpoints in the National Provider Directory." - Context: Core position on API endpoint reporting.
2. "We do not support the alternative approach of self-publication through NDH IG Endpoint Profile." - Context: Objection to decentralized endpoint discovery.
3. "There remains an urgent need for a clear network-based product identifier." - Context: Recommendation for structured network/plan/payer identifiers.
4. "CMS should require reporting aggregated denial rates broken out by such reason codes." - Context: Request for coded PA denial reporting.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - The comment focuses on giving consumers access to correct plan, provider, formulary, price, and PA information.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - It discusses specific implementation mechanisms including NPD collection, endpoint URLs, FHIR Formulary, X12 codes, and ONC Lantern-like monitoring.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - The comment calls for structured identifiers and use of existing X12 and FHIR standards while acknowledging areas needing further development.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Endpoint publication, TIC URLs, identifiers, formularies, and denial reason reporting are all transparency-focused.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The recommendations require coordination among CMS, payers, app developers, consumers, the Department of Labor, and market segments outside CMS's direct reach.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The comment is grounded in Checkbook's real-world data collection workflows and payer URL discovery problems.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - It addresses app developers, price transparency vendors, and entities building plan shopping tools.
- [x] **FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS** - The comment supports consistent consumer access across QHP and non-QHP market segments, including broader commercial markets.
